paragraphs.text: Hey, guys, and welcome to a special Patreon episode of Tis the Podcast. I'm Julia. I'm Anthony. I'm Thom. I'm excited to see y'all on a night we don't usually record. Twice in one week. You're talking about something we usually don't talk about? That's right. Halloween!

I'm always excited about that. I actually just, like, five minutes before we started recording tonight, got back from driving around in a while. I'm also looking at people's Halloween decorations with the three boys and Marty. Hannah was not interested. So wouldn't it be the four boys? It would be, yeah. Yeah, it would be the four boys. I do commonly refer to them as my four boys. So do the kids and Marty prefer the scary or the, like, cute, the more cutesy?

So, yes, I know exactly what you mean. And so Gabe and Ethan prefer the scary. Marty's probably split down the middle and Jude likes the cute. Because we were driving around and he'd see a ghost and he'd go, that's Gary dosed. That's Gary ghost. Like, yeah, I know. It is kind of scary. But then he'd see orange lights and he'd freak out because they were orange lights. So we don't have many people participating in decorating here in Owasso. So I feel like I've noticed that here. Like, I feel like Halloween, like, kind of gets less of a big deal every year. You think it's getting edged out by Christmas? I think Christmas creep is, yeah. Uh-oh. It's like everybody out there that gripes about Christmas stuff coming out too early.
This is them. They're shaking their fists in the air and they're going, see? They are.

I wonder if that's it. Well, maybe if Halloween put out more content like Christmas does, it would have more staying power. It's like Dunder and Blixom commented on our Hocus Pocus episode. There just isn't a lot of movies about Halloween. You know, it's hard to find anything that sparks as much excitement as the birth of God, you know? Or, you know, an old man sliding down a chimney and leaving you free stuff. That's exciting. I'm glad that's what's exciting to you. I'll stick with my Jesus. Oh, my gosh.
Well, you know. Hashtag not subtle judgment. You know what's exciting about Halloween that doesn't get enough credit? It's the visit of the Great Pumpkin every year, guys. That's true.

That's very true. So if you have young ones listening, you may want to send them away real quick. Because I'm going to unfortunately tell you there is no Great Pumpkin, Anthony. You just don't believe hard enough because he's appeared in my pumpkin patch before. It's because your pumpkin patch is so sincere. I'm going to call BS. I don't think you could have a more sincere pumpkin patch than Linus.
I would totally agree with that. What?
No way. You cannot compete with Linus when it comes to sincerity. Yeah, he is the ultimate sincerest. I feel like I can. And I feel like I embody more of the Linus moment than Linus himself.
I have some… this movie is going to bring me to some discussions about Linus moments, with Linus, and the paradox we create here. But yeah, we'll get to that later.
We'll be right back.

Okay. So if you haven't figured it out yet, what we're discussing tonight is a 1966 TV short. So not a movie, a TV short: It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown. A classic. I'm going to say it, because I don't think anybody's going to argue with me: it's a classic Halloween short. For those of you who are not familiar with this one, I'm going to tell you, go watch it. It's worth it. But we'll also do a teeny-tiny baby synopsis. If you're familiar with the Peanuts gang… when I refer to the Peanuts, I mean Charlie Brown, Linus, Sally, and the whole crew.
Snoopy, Woodstock.

Yes, that's the Peanuts. So for this one, the Peanuts gang celebrates Halloween, with Linus hoping that finally he will be visited by the Great Pumpkin, while Charlie Brown is invited to a Halloween party.
That's a terrible synopsis.
Oh my God.
Accidentally invited.
No, no. I can't wait to talk about Charlie Brown's Halloween party and trick-or-treating.

Okay, let's do this one. Let's do this one. Charlie Brown is excited to be invited to his first-ever party, Violet's Halloween party. Before the party, the Peanuts gang plans to go trick-or-treating with Snoopy, who is dressed as the World War I Flying Ace, taking his Halloween persona to an extreme. The one person who won't be joining them for tricks or treats or the party is Linus, who will be waiting in his local pumpkin patch for the arrival of the Great Pumpkin. Linus believes that the Great Pumpkin rises out of the most sincere pumpkin patch, none more sincere than his own local one, flies into the air, and delivers presents to all the boys and girls around the world. Because of his belief, Linus is the laughingstock among his friends. Sally is torn between going trick-or-treating for the first time and attending Violet's surefire-fun Halloween party, or following her love, Linus, and waiting for the Great Pumpkin's arrival with him.
That's solid. That's much better.
That is also very in-depth.
It is in-depth for a Peanuts flick.

Well, we're keeping in the Halloween spirit. Okay, so it's the same cast we've covered, so we're not going to linger much on the cast. It's still directed by Bill Melendez and written by Charles Schulz. If you've joined us on Tis the Podcast, which we hope you have, if you've made your way to Patreon as well: we have covered, oh my gosh, A Charlie Brown Christmas. We have covered A Charlie Brown Christmas, and we actually had a really cool guest host on that episode, and I would encourage you to check that one out. It's an early Tis the Podcast episode, so go check it out in our library. It's worth a listen.
And we mean early. That was like episode seven or eight.
I'm thinking next year may be time to revisit A Charlie Brown Christmas.
Oh, interesting.
I'm voting nay.
What'd you say?
I'm voting nay.
Why?
I just don't really want to have to revisit it.
Don't want to have to, or don't think it's necessary? Because I could see both.
Yeah. That's something where maybe we can just be like, no, let's just leave it.

I think what we should do, if we have a bunch of those we want to revisit, is a special Patreon episode where we do a retrospective, or a live watch with fans. We can now do that with our Facebook group.
Oh, we can?
Yes. You can start a watch party.
That is awesome. That needs to happen.
Does that mean this year we're finally going to do the live watch of the tree lighting?
We need to. I mean, I think that would be super-duper fun.
I think that'd be fun. Just riffing.
Yeah, just riffing for however long it is, with all the musical guests and stuff. I think that'd be a lot of fun.
Oh, that's right, because they do all the things too. I never watched that. I think the first time I watched it was last year.
Yep, yep. And Diana Krall was on it, right?
Yep. I love her, but she's a little awkward.
So I say we do that. I say we create a poll or something and see who would be interested in doing that.
Yeah, let's create a poll. Polls are good.

Okay. So I want to know y'all's history with this special. We talked about that with the Christmas one, but let's talk about your history with It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown. Anthony, you want to go first?

Sure. Just like I don't remember a Christmas without A Charlie Brown Christmas, I don't remember a Halloween without It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown. I mean, the Peanuts embody the holidays for me. I know they're a thing outside of the holidays, but when I think of the Peanuts, I just think of the holiday specials, especially these two, more than Thanksgiving and New Year's and Valentine's Day and all that. These two are undisputed classics in my mind. And I'm sure we'll talk about this later, so I'm not going to say which one I think is better, but while I give one the edge, that doesn't take anything away from the other one. It's right there with it. And you will find a lot of people who would argue the other one's better, because last year, on the Tis the Podcast Twitter, there was a huge debate between people on Twitter about which of these two specials is better. But yeah, I love It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown. I really do. And I can't wait for it to air on ABC this year. Even though I own it, it's just more special to catch it on TV with the commercials. It feels more in season.
Yeah, it does.
When it's on, that means it's socially accepted.
I feel that way about all the Christmas stuff too. I own my Charlie Brown Christmas and Rankin/Bass, but I get so excited when I catch them on TV.
Yeah, yeah. I do too. What's your history, Thom?

I have a history that goes beyond memory. I don't remember not knowing this TV special. I remember it as a kid. I always liked to watch it. For some reason, I remember it was on CBS. Still to this day, from my childhood, I remember the CBS commercials that came on and everything. I was a big fan as a kid. This one, sans the Red Baron foolishness, I think I like more than the Christmas one, honestly.
Are we just revealing that right now? I thought we were going to do that later on.
I'll amend my statement, then, to say I prefer the Christmas one.
Oh, that's funny.
I give the Christmas one a slight edge, I think because of the music.
That's fair. That's fair. And it being Christmas.
I get it. I just find the Christmas one boring. I think I talked about that in an episode too.
Yeah. And then you said you created beautiful memories with Ellie and scored it high.
I did, because she liked it, not because I did. But because I have these memories of her now, it's something we watch every year together.
You know, Julia, before this devolves into a fight because Thom is angering me, what is your history with this?
I'm not… no, I'm in the same boat. I'm not going to say I don't enjoy watching it. I just end up doing other things while it's on. The Christmas one always becomes more of a background for me.

Well, I think the Christmas one can be more of a background just by virtue of the music. It has a little bit of a background quality to it. And I don't know of a complete Christmas playlist that exists without Vince's music, right? His music has become so iconic with the Christmas season that even the non-traditional Christmas songs are now Christmas songs.
Yep. What's your history, Julia?

Same as y'all's. I don't remember Halloween without it. I remember the excitement of seeing it come on TV. It made it really feel like Halloween was upon us, the same way the Christmas and Thanksgiving ones would as well. My brother loved Peanuts first and instilled the love in me. As far as which I like better, I like the Christmas one better, because the storyline is a lot more poignant to me, right? It's more serious. They cover some more serious things in the Christmas one, which I really enjoy, so it gives me more of the feels. But from a fun perspective, this one by far beats the Christmas one.

It's funny. To your point, Julia, about being more poignant, I feel like the Christmas one also has more of a story, where this one is a little more… I don't want to say episodic, because there's this overarching story, but it doesn't flow as well, maybe. It's not as flowy. You know what I'm trying to say. I don't want to use the word cohesive, because it's cohesive. I think the Christmas one was tighter. I'll say that.
This one is choppy.
Yes. Yeah, that's a good word for it.

Yeah. It's funny, Jude has just gotten into Charlie Brown, and he really, really, really loves It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, and he just kind of tolerates the Christmas one, because there are definitely moments in the Christmas one that are a little slower, right? They don't keep a kid's attention. And even me, like Thom said, I'll drift off and have it in the background. I love it so much, but there are moments where it's a bit slow. So I think if you asked any kid, they'd probably like this one better.
You should get Jude to record something about this one for us.
Oh, I'll see what I can do. I'll see what I can do about that.
Okay. So it's a pretty short and sweet story, right? The synopsis kind of covered it.
I don't know if I would call it a sweet story. I'd call it a short story.

Yeah. There's not a ton of sweetness in this one. We still have Charlie Brown, who's getting the short stick every time. He's invited accidentally to a Halloween party, which he is fine with, because he's invited. He doesn't care that it's an accident. He got an invitation.

And that's a nice callback to the Christmas one, where he gets a Christmas card, and he sarcastically thanks a girl for the Christmas card, because he got none. And the girl's like, "I didn't send you a Christmas card, Charlie Brown." "Doesn't anyone understand sarcasm anymore?"
These kids are still so mean.
They're so mean.
It always makes me laugh when they go out for tricks or treats and he gets a rock every time. I feel so bad for him, but it's just so funny.
Yeah. "I got a popcorn ball." "I got a candy bar." "I got a piece of chocolate." "I got a rock."
So I've got an interesting behind-the-scenes thing about that.
Oh, what?
After the special originally aired in the '60s, children all over the country sent candy to Charlie Brown at the studio it aired on, out of sympathy, because he didn't get any.
That is so sweet.
They're so kind, if we just let them be.
That's right.
They are not the kids in these shows.
No. Lucy, sure. Yeah, she is a jerk. And Sally is high-strung.
Okay, I will agree with Sally. I don't agree about Lucy.
She's a jerk.
I don't think Lucy's a jerk.
No, no, no, no. She's a jerk.

But she has a sweet moment in this, when she goes to the pumpkin patch and brings Linus home in the middle of the night and takes off his shoes. I think that's probably one of the sweetest Lucy moments in any of these specials, if not the sweetest.
Charlie Brown moments… all the kids are mean. They're very violent children.

So we talked about this during the Christmas special. I brought up how I'm always surprised, given how much of a staple Woodstock is in Christmas decorations, that he's not in the Christmas special. And Woodstock's not in the Halloween special either, even though all the Peanuts Halloween stuff in stores, all the merchandise, includes Woodstock now.
He is in the Thanksgiving one, though.
He is. Should we cover that on Patreon maybe next?

Yes, because I love the Thanksgiving one. Spoiler alert, that's what I'm going to do for Thanksgiving dinner: we're going to do a Charlie Brown Thanksgiving dinner this year, and it's going to be jelly beans, toast, popcorn, and I don't remember the other thing.
Are you really? Awesome.
Yeah. We're going to put it in our Advent activities. The kids don't know yet. It'll technically be after Thanksgiving.
But that's so cool.
Yeah, that'd be fun. They won't know what's happening, because they don't love A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving like I do.
What if my brother's there? He would get it.
Yeah, yeah. I don't know why Woodstock's not in this one.
He came later anyway.
Yeah. Well, what year did Thanksgiving come out? I'm going to look it up right now. This one's '66, so Woodstock was invented, and he first appeared March 4th,
1966. So this would have been animated and everything before he appeared.
Oh. By the time he appeared.

And he wasn't given a name until after the Woodstock festival, which they named him after. So he appeared in the comic strip in 1966 for the first time. His first appearance on film was in Snoopy Come Home, in 1972.
Oh, that movie makes me cry and cry and cry.
Me too. I love that one. That one's so sad.
Okay. So I don't even know what we're talking about.
Oh yeah. "I got a rock."

We have the side storyline where Sally is still in love with Linus. And Linus is very confusing to me in this TV short, because how are you not wrapped up in the Santa-ness of Christmas? You remember Christmas and what Christmas is about, but then you believe this Great Pumpkin mythology, which is not mythology to him, at Halloween time. I don't understand that. When you put the two next to each other, these two Linuses are different people.

Well, okay. I'm going to say that Linus definitely had a grasp on what the Christmas season was about, but they never said he wasn't into Santa. He just had a better grasp of what the Christmas season was actually about.
I got a very strong impression that he wasn't about Santa.
Yeah. These Linuses feel different. I'm not going to say jerky, but this one feels more immature.
Yes, this one feels more immature. The one in the Christmas one feels much older, right?

Absolutely. There's more wisdom, definitely. And it's not just the moment when he stands on the stage in the Christmas one and has the wisdom. The whole episode, he seems older in spirit than the rest of them.
Well, it would have made more sense chronologically if this one came first, and this one knocked some maturity into him, right?
That's true. He gets burned, and the pumpkin patch brings about some personal growth, where by the time he gets to Christmas, he's like, "Look, guys, don't believe your dreams."
Jaded Linus.

Yeah. So Linus spends every Halloween missing tricks or treats and missing the party, because he's sitting in a pumpkin patch waiting for the Great Pumpkin to show up and give gifts to everybody around the world. But he only shows up in the sincere pumpkin patches. And like Thom said earlier, this would be the most sincere pumpkin patch just because Linus is there. He's a sincere guy.
He is a sincere guy. He's a sweet guy.
He's a sweet guy. I like Linus.
Spoiler alert: the Great Pumpkin does not show up, and Linus is upset. But Sally is downright nuclear.
Sally feels as though she's been… nuclear. "It's pronounced nucular." That's a Homer quote for you.
No, Sally is me.
Nobody forced her to stay. She just chose to.
And she does it for the wrong reason.
Not at all. No, no.
I have a little behind-the-scenes trivia about Sally in this one.
Oh.

So the actress who does Sally's voice, Kathy Steinberg, had almost finished recording all of her lines of dialogue when the producers got a phone call saying that her tooth was loose and about to fall out. They thought she'd have a sudden lisp, so they rushed her back to the studio to finish recording her last lines, and right as she finished her last take, the tooth fell out.
Oh my goodness.
That's dedication for a kid.
Yeah. Kid actors, huh? The stuff you've got to think about.
Yep. That's interesting. I love the voices in these. They're always so great. And again, because they're real kids, right? It gives them…
Yeah. And you can tell with this one, though, that all the kids can read now.
Yes. You can tell. You can tell that.

So, Thom, you mentioned the Red Baron bit of nonsense. So the Red Baron that Thom is alluding to: Snoopy has a bit in the middle, I guess kind of throughout, but mostly in the middle, where he's the Red Baron on his… well, where he's fighting the Red Baron.
Oh, he's fighting the Red Baron. Sorry.
Yeah, he's fighting the Red Baron on his doghouse. And you think that's a bit of nonsense?
Oh, I can't stand it. It drives me nuts. It drags on so long. It doesn't add anything to the story.
I will agree it went on a little long, but I love Snoopy's fantasies.
Yeah, it makes me… I don't.

So did you guys see the new Peanuts movie? The theatrical one, from a few years back? First of all, it's awesome. Like, you guys are Peanuts fans. Schulz's kid was involved in it, so he made sure they kept it on brand. But the Red Baron stuff in that was done so well.
Really?
Yeah.
I mean, shocker. I saw the animation style in the previews, and I was like, I don't want to see it.
Me too. That's why I didn't watch it either.

Yeah. No, you guys have got to give it a chance. It's on HBO, for free, if you have the channel. It's on demand, is what I meant. But even though they have that animation, they still move the same way. They don't turn more than they turn in the originals.
Okay. Yeah, that's good.
So it's not just completely different now. Again, Schulz's kid was involved, and he did a really good job of making sure that it stayed true.
I'll have to check it out. It might be a movie-night movie for the Colburn household.
It's a good family movie night movie.

I think I could stomach watching it. I mean, I like the Red Baron part. Anything Snoopy does on his doghouse always cracks me up. I like it when he shoots people off the top of it. It's just hilarious to me.
My favorite is when he's the vulture. Vulture Snoopy is one of my favorite gags he does, especially when he's messing with Lucy, because it drives her absolutely insane.

I love when Lucy messes with Charlie Brown and rips the football away. I always love that. So, for those of you… I own the digital copy of this one, so it comes with a bunch of those extra Snoopy bits, or Peanuts bits, you've never seen ever. And one of them is The Magician. It's a TV short about a magician. So Snoopy does a bit of magic, and he actually turns Charlie Brown invisible, and invisible Charlie Brown ends up actually kicking the football. I rarely love those extra ones. The pilgrim one I'm not really a fan of. It feels like it drags on, but they always play it after the Thanksgiving one. But The Magician one was pretty cute. I really kind of liked it. And then they have some disco Snoopy one. Did you see that one? It's like Flashdance.
Oh my God.
It's pretty amazing, I'm not going to lie.
So did you know the football… this is the first time it was ever animated? It was always in the comic strip, but this is the first film it appeared in.
Really? Pulling the football away from Charlie Brown?
Yep.
They make it seem like it's just an old gag in this.
Yeah. Which, I guess, in the life of the strip, it was a gag by that point.
It makes me feel terrible and laugh at the same time, every time.
Why is he so excited about kicking the football? I don't get it.

Because he doesn't get a bunch of wins in his life, and the satisfaction of kicking a ball is the same as hitting a ball in baseball. When you actually make contact, it feels like a win. Charlie Brown, yeah.
But they have little holders that you could buy. You just buy that, do it, and be done with it.
He's a kid. He doesn't have that kind of cash. He's got to rely on Lucy for that.
So it's pretty iconic when it comes to Halloween: the Peanuts dress-up costumes, I think.
Yep. You can see those pictures taken out of context, and you know it's Peanuts.
Oh, I love that music when they're trick-or-treating, especially at the beginning, before the title card comes up, when the ghosts actually seem scary, just a little bit, at the beginning.
Yeah, yeah. I like that Charlie Brown's sheet ghost ended up with a whole bunch of eyes, because he had trouble with the scissors.
I love that they use his bald head as a model for their jack-o'-lanterns. I remember thinking that was just so mean.
Yeah. And then you get to see Charlie Brown's reaction. He's just so red in the face, and he looks furious.
That's funny. Oh my gosh, I love it. "Tricks or treats." "Tricks or treats" was one of my favorites, y'all.
"Tricks or treats." Yeah, I love the "tricks or treats."

That's most of the parts. And then we have the end, where Charlie Brown's actually talking to Linus about disappointment. Linus is exhausted, and he's really upset that the Great Pumpkin didn't show up, and he's stressing about it. And Charlie Brown makes this offhand comment, like, "I've believed in some dumb stuff myself," and Linus loses his crap.
Oh my God. You're like, dude, Linus, chill, man.
And I love that they play the credits as Linus is just ranting and raving.
Yes, yes. As the ranter and raver of this podcast, I could relate to him in that moment.
Just on this podcast, Anthony?
Just on this podcast.
Huh. Okay. You neither rant nor rave in any other part of your life?
No.
I love that. There is something about a Peanuts rant and rave. Sally's rant goes on quite a long time, when she realizes there's no such thing as the Great Pumpkin.
Yeah. Hers just perpetuates, and then so does his.
"I'm going to sue you."
Yeah. I like that line. "I'm going to sue you."
Yeah, it's good.
Well, before we get to quotes, I have a question: is this a Christmas movie? Does it pass the Linus test?
No.
Linus does not pass his own test. That's why this got so meta.
He just learns nothing.
Quotes. Yeah, let's do quotes. Favorite quotes, favorite scenes.

So I loved when Linus was like, "There are three things I've learned never to discuss with people: religion, politics, and the Great Pumpkin." And all I can think about with the first two is how times have changed since back then.
A lot of people still won't do it, man.
I'm just saying, it's more common now, with social media. We just don't care.

Oh, that's funny. I think it still holds true for in-person contact, which would have been the only contact Linus is referring to, because they didn't have that kind of stuff. So I like… sorry, you go.
No, you go.
When Lucy puts on her witch costume, and she's like, "A person should always choose a costume which is in direct contrast to her own personality," and everybody laughs.

I like, at the very beginning, you see Lucy and Linus with a big pumpkin. They go out of their house, they get a big pumpkin, they bring it back into their house, they lay the paper down, they put the pumpkin on top, and then Lucy busts out this big old knife and starts hacking the top of it off, and she starts scooping the guts out. And Linus goes, "You didn't tell me you were going to kill it!" Which Jude will quote now.
Really?
Oh, that's awesome, dude.
Do any of your kids actually get upset when you cut up the pumpkin?
No. In the odd case that we do cut up a pumpkin, they don't get upset. Does Ellie?
Don't you do pumpkins?
No. I forget about it, and then we never get around to it. So no, we don't carve pumpkins anymore.
We did it last weekend, and Ellie loved it.
Yeah? Did you do a standard jack-o'-lantern face?
That's what she wanted.
Oh, I love that. She's a Halloween purist.
She is. That's why she wants to be a ghost, as she says.

So I like Sally's little rant: "I was robbed! I spent the whole night waiting for the Great Pumpkin when I could have been out for tricks or treats. Halloween is over, and I missed it! You blockhead!" Which I find interesting, that she called Linus a blockhead, because that's usually Charlie's insult, right? "You kept me up all night waiting for the Great Pumpkin, and all that came was a beagle! I didn't get a chance to go out for tricks or treats, and it was all your fault! I'll sue! What a fool I was. I could have had candy apples and gum and cookies and money and all sorts of things, but no! I had to listen to you! You blockhead! What a fool I was. Tricks or treats come only once a year, and I missed it by sitting in a pumpkin patch with a blockhead. You owe me restitution!"
She's so angry.
I like it after that, when Snoopy rises from the patch, and Linus is so excited, because he thinks it's the Great Pumpkin, and he passes out.
I like where Linus says, "You've heard of the fury of a woman scorned, haven't you? Well, that's nothing compared to the fury of a woman who has been cheated out of tricks or treats."

I'll tackle the quote that ties this into our regular podcast with a Christmas reference. So Charlie and Linus are sitting next to each other. Charlie says, "Who are you writing to, Linus?" Linus says, "This is the time of year to write to the Great Pumpkin. On Halloween night, the Great Pumpkin rises out of his pumpkin patch and flies through the air with his bag of toys for all the children." Charlie says, "You must be crazy. When are you going to stop believing in something that isn't true?" "When you stop believing in that fellow with the red suit and the white beard who goes, 'Ho, ho, ho.'" And Charlie says, "We are obviously separated by denominational differences."
And to tie it back to the Christmas special, Snoopy once again licks Lucy, and she's like, "Ugh! Dog germs!"

I love this conversation between Linus and Sally. Linus says, "He'll come here, because I have the most sincere pumpkin patch, and he respects sincerity." And Sally says, "Do you really think he'll come?" And Linus says, "Tonight the Great Pumpkin will rise out of the pumpkin patch. He flies through the air and brings toys to all the children of the world." And Sally says, "That's a good story." And Linus says, "You don't believe the story of the Great Pumpkin? I thought little girls always believed everything that was told to them. I thought little girls were innocent and trusting." And Sally says, "Welcome to the 20th century."

This weird new Linus, who has somehow become a changeling for our original Linus, asks people about singing pumpkin carols, which I thought was weird, because we don't sing Santa carols, right? I would think they'd be Halloween carols. But, you know. Oh boy.

Okay, so going back to the football bit, since this is the first time it appeared in animation. Charlie's like, "You just want me to come running up to kick that ball so you can pull it away and see me land flat on my back and kill myself." And Lucy says, "This time you can trust me. See, here's a signed document testifying that I promise not to pull it away." And Charlie Brown says, "It is signed. It's a signed document. I guess if you have a signed document in your possession, you can't go wrong. This year I'm really going to kick that football." And then he runs to kick the football, Lucy pulls it away, and he does his little "Aaugh!" as he falls down. And Lucy's like, "Peculiar thing about this document: it was never notarized."
She's such a punk.
She is awful.
We don't rank our Halloween ones. I mean, we usually give a score just to see what it would average, but we don't keep track of them. What would you guys give it?
Six.
I'm going ten.
I'm going nine. That's the perfect Halloween bit.
So 25 divided by three.
Sounds complicated.
Eight and a third.
Fractions.
I think. Yep. There you go.

So this would rank eight and a third, which is below A Charlie Brown Christmas, if we're going to compare them. I put up a poll an hour ago in our new Facebook group, and surprisingly a lot of people responded to it, just asking what our listeners preferred: A Charlie Brown Christmas or It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown. 35 people picked A Charlie Brown Christmas, two people picked It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, and a listener, Craig Brewer, wrote in his own answer, You're Elected, Charlie Brown, and two people voted for that.
